Love to the Uttermost gives expositions of John chapters thirteen through twenty-one, dated 1898. Those chapters cover Christ's last night with his disciples and beyond. The commentary begins, though, in the Temple courts of older worship.

Two objects met the entering worshipper there: the Brazen Altar and the Laver. The Laver stood always full of pure, fresh water. Priests washed there before their consecration for holy work. They washed before putting on the robes of sacred office. From such types, the expositions move to Christ's washing of feet. Readers get careful verse-by-verse teaching. It serves study of John's Gospel in a devout, detailed style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict: Benedict XI was the Dominican pope whose eight months ended at Perugia. This entry traces his pontificate, his peace-making, and his death. The friar on Peter's throne: his humble tomb at Perugia still draws pilgrims today in humble prayerful devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-: Clement XI was the Albani pope of the Jansenist and Chinese rites controversies. This entry traces his long pontificate, his bulls, and his trials. The pope of Unigenitus: his famous bull condemned the stubborn Jansenists of wayward France forevermore in 1713.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-: Gregory XI was the pope who brought the papacy home from Avignon. This entry traces his pontificate, his return, and his death. The last of the Avignon popes: his fateful return doomed the brief schism's peace in fatal 1378 forever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent: Innocent XI was the blessed Odescalchi pope who defied Louis XIV. This entry traces his pontificate, his reforms, and his sanctity. The saint of the anti-nepotism age: his lavish alms emptied the papal treasury for the Roman poor daily in love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xi: John XI was the pope who was Marozia's son, raised to the throne by his mother. This entry traces his pontificate, his bondage, and his times. The pope of the Theophylact tyranny: his imperious mother's will was law in Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-xi: Leo XI was the pope whose reign lasted twenty-six days in 1605. This entry traces his election, his brief days, and his death. The pope of a single April: his sudden election thrilled the hopeful Medici kin in Medicean Florence.

podcast-joerogan-XN-sk8dE9xI:
A statue that holds a mummified monk inside it is the subject of a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Scans of an ancient Chinese Buddha statue revealed a seated human skeleton within, a monk who may have mummified himself through a grim ritual years long.

Rogan works through the discovery and the practice behind it, in which monks slowly starved and preserved their own bodies as acts of devotion. The talk asks what such faith asks of a person. The segment is a short, eerie piece of religious history, the kind of true oddity the show loves to pass along.
podcast-tuckercarlson-REEtJTqJbxI:
Journalist Matt Taibbi joins Tucker Carlson to discuss the secret files President Trump has been releasing. Taibbi, famous for his work on the Twitter Files, champions full declassification of government records. Here he argues for what should come out next.

Taibbi lists the files he most wants opened, from assassination records to intelligence abuses. He explains how secrecy protects officials more than it protects the country. Carlson asks whether Trump will really follow through against agency resistance. Curious viewers get a reporter's map of the vaults and a case for throwing them open.
un-ga-res-2200-xxi:
Adopted on December 16, 1966, General Assembly Resolution 2200 (XXI) gave the world its two great human rights covenants. The Roman numeral marks the Assembly's twenty-first session. Catalog copies that date it to 1948 are wrong; 1948 brought the Universal Declaration, while the binding treaties came eighteen years later.

One covenant guards civil and political rights, such as free speech and fair trials. The other covers work, health, schooling, and a fair standard of living. A third short text let people appeal to a UN body about abuses. States then signed and ratified the pair over the next decade, and they still anchor rights law today.
